title: Kafka: hot partitions
seriesDescription: A Kafka deep dive for system design interviews: why Kafka exists, terminology, messages and keys, offsets and replication, when to use it, scalability, hot partitions, fault tolerance, retries, performance and retention.
description: What a hot partition is and the four fixes, each with the trade-off an interviewer wants to hear.
source: Study notes: Kafka deep dive for system design interviews

questions.prompt: Every click for one very popular ad uses the same key. What is the effect?

options.text: One partition is overwhelmed while the others sit nearly idle: a hot partition.
options.why: Right: a skewed key makes a bottleneck.

options.text: The clicks are spread perfectly evenly in the majority of deployments.
options.why: The opposite happens; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Kafka automatically splits the ad across partitions.
options.why: Kafka does not do that on its own.

options.text: The clicks are dropped as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: They are all sent to one partition.

questions.prompt: What is the cost of dropping the key to spread load?

options.text: You lose the ordering guarantee for related messages.
options.why: Right: fine if ordering does not matter.

options.text: The messages become larger without any extra configuration.
options.why: Size is unchanged; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Kafka stops accepting writes.
options.why: It accepts them; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Consumers can no longer join groups.
options.why: Unrelated; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: A good choice when ordering is not needed.

questions.prompt: You add a random number to the ad id in the key. What is the downside?

options.text: One ad's clicks are split across partitions, so aggregation gets harder and the consumer must combine them.
options.why: Right: balance costs simplicity.

options.text: Messages for the same ad are now guaranteed to be in order without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: Order is weaker; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The key can no longer be hashed for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: It can; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Kafka rejects keys with numbers.
options.why: It does not; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.prompt: When does a compound key such as ad id plus region work best?

options.text: When you can find an attribute that varies independently of the ad id.
options.why: Right: traffic then spreads more evenly.

options.text: When all clicks come from one region in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: Then it does not spread.

options.text: When the region changes each second in a typical production setup.
options.why: Keys should be stable.

options.text: When you have no attribute to add.
options.why: You need one; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: It keeps some grouping while spreading load.

questions.prompt: What is back pressure as a hot partition fix?

options.text: Slow the producer when the partition lag is too high; use it when producers may be throttled.
options.why: Right: the easy fix when you cannot change the key.

options.text: Add more consumers than partitions in the group for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Extra consumers sit idle.

options.text: Delete the hot partition.
options.why: That loses data; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Speed the producer up to clear the lag as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: That worsens it; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: A managed service may have built-in mechanisms.

questions.prompt: True or false: a skewed key creates hot partitions, while a good key spreads load evenly across partitions.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the key decides how evenly the load spreads.

options.text: False
options.why: The key is what decides the spread.

questions.explanation: The key is your main tool for balance, and a bad one is the usual cause of hot partitions.

questions.prompt: Ordering is not needed, but you still want one popular ad spread across partitions. Which fix is the simplest?

options.text: Drop the key and let the default partitioner spread messages.
options.why: Right: ordering is not needed.

options.text: Add a compound key with unrelated data without any extra configuration.
options.why: Unneeded work; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Apply back pressure to all producers in a typical production setup.
options.why: It throttles everyone.

options.text: Make the topic a single partition.
options.why: That concentrates load.

questions.explanation: Name two or three fixes and say what each one costs.
